title: Numerical Sayings
aka: for three transgressions and for four
lead: A numerical saying counts its subject with two numbers in a row ("three things... four", "six... seven"), then lists the items, often saving the most striking for last. The form appears in Proverbs, Amos, Job, Micah and Sirach, and before Israel in the poems of Ugarit.

sections.b:
The pattern names a number and then one more: "The LORD hates six things, / and seven are abhorrent to his very self" (Proverbs 6:16–19). Proverbs 30 has four such sayings (30:15–16, 18–19, 21–23, 29–31) and one plain list of four (30:24–28). The prophet Amos uses the form to open each of his oracles against the nations, "for three crimes... and for four" (Amos 1:3–2:6). Eliphaz promises rescue "through six troubles... and in seven" (Job 5:19). Micah speaks of "seven shepherds, eight leaders" (Micah 5:5), and Sirach has several (Sirach 25:7–11; Sirach 26:5–6, 28; Sirach 50:25–26). The second number shows that the list is full, and the last item often carries the point.

The form is older than Israel. A Ugaritic poem says Baal hates two kinds of feast, three the Rider of the Clouds (KTU 1.4 iii 17–21), and the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar has "two things are good, and a third is pleasing to Shamash".
